# AppWithAI — model office hours

> **One document for building or changing a business application with EML.**
> Read it, then run office hours with the person in front of you: work their
> business through with them, one decision at a time, and hand back one file —
> `<business-name>.mmd`, every byte of it Mermaid, accepted by the published
> checker — from which the generator builds the whole application: its data, its
> forms, its rules, its workflows and who may do what.
>
> **New or change is decided by one fact: did they give you a `.mmd`?** With a
> model attached or pasted, you are changing that model — whole, in place, losing
> nothing. Without one, you are building a new one from their description. §1
> is the procedure for both; §1.1.1 decides which you are in. **Either way, the
> first work is research, not drafting** (§1.1.2.1): put on your thinking cap,
> research the domain as widely as you can, then attack your own research
> adversarially — and only then start building and reviewing with the user.

- **EML version**: 1.2.0 · **Based on**: Mermaid · **Updated**: 2026-10-20
- **This document**: `https://www.appwithai.org/llms.txt`
- **Authority**: `language/appwithai-language.json`. Where this document and that
  file disagree, that file wins.
- **Validators** (§8): `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/checker.js` and
  `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/fixer.js`. **Write that exact form every
  time** — scheme included, `www.` included, and never a bare host. The apex
  `https://appwithai.org` serves the same files, but the `www.` form is the canonical one.
  **If the host is not reachable from your environment, that is a
  fact about your network and not a reason to skip validation or to stop** —
  §8.4's last two rows are the offline procedure, and they are real runs with
  real counts.
- **Validation is mandatory, and it is two runs, not one.** Before you hand over a
  model you run the checker **and** the audit (§8.5) on the file's own bytes, and
  your delivery reports both verdicts, verbatim. A model that was not run through
  both is not delivered, it is a draft. Do not offer the run, do not defer it to the
  user, do not replace it with a review of your own, and never report counts you did
  not get from a run. Every environment has a route that works (§8.4); finding it is
  part of the job. Only when every route is exhausted does §1.3.5 apply, and it
  changes what you may claim, not whether you tried.
- **To check a model from a shell** (§1.3, §8.4) — nothing to install:
  `curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/check-model.mjs` then
  `node check-model.mjs my-business.mmd`. Exit `0` means the generator accepts
  it; exit `1` means it does not, and the report says why.
- **To check whether it is *finished*** (§8.5, §10) — a different question, and
  the one a clean report does not answer:
  `curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/audit-model.mjs` then
  `node audit-model.mjs my-business.mmd`. It scores the model against §10's
  checklist — every reference column's `FK` modifier, every enum binding, help on
  every entity, column and section, every form laid out in sections, a state
  machine per lifecycle, `%%rbac` on every entity — and exits `0` only when all
  of it is there. **A bare ERD passes the checker with zero errors and fails
  this audit nine ways.** Run both before you deliver.
- **The Application Dictionary is mandatory, all of it** (§3.7): a lookup for
  every reference, a dropdown for every closed vocabulary, help on every entity,
  column and section, and **every form laid out as headed sections of two-column
  rows**. Nothing after authoring adds a value you leave out.
- **Every example in this document is a complete model that the checker accepts
  with zero errors and zero warnings.** Paste any of them into `check()` and see.
  Imitate their shape.
- **The commonest failure is answering with prose about the model instead of the
  model.** A reply of headings, bullet lists and an entity glossary is not a
  model however thorough it is: the checker reads it as empty and returns
  `EML004`. The second commonest, when you were given a model, is handing back
  only the part that changed. §1.0 exists to stop both; read it before you start.

---

## 0. What EML is

An EML document is **valid Mermaid**. It renders as diagrams in any Mermaid
viewer, on GitHub, in an editor preview — and the same bytes compile into a
complete application. Everything the language adds rides in Mermaid comments
(`%%`), which renderers ignore and the compiler reads.

That is the whole idea. One file, readable as a picture and executable as a
specification. Three kinds of diagram carry three layers of the application:

| You draw | It defines |
|---|---|
| `erDiagram` | Every entity, attribute, key and relationship |
| `flowchart` marked `kind: rules` | The decisions the business makes, and the actions they take |
| `stateDiagram-v2` | The lifecycle a record moves through, and who may move it |

A model that uses only `erDiagram` is a valid model. Rules and workflows are
additions to it, not prerequisites.

**File extensions**: `.mmd`, and the qualified variants `.eml.mmd`, `.erd.mmd`,
`.flow.mmd`, `.rules.mmd` — all read identically. Encoding is UTF-8. Deliver as
`<business-name>.mmd` (§1.2); the variants exist for files kept in a repository
beside other Mermaid, not for handing to a user. `.md` is not an EML file, and a
model saved as one is a model nothing on the receiving end will run.

---

## 1. Office hours — how to answer "build me an app" and "change my model"

This section is the **procedure**, and it governs. It is one procedure for both
requests a person brings to a model of their business: *build me one* and
*change the one I have*. Whatever words they use, carry out their instruction
*within* these guidelines rather than in place of them. Their words set the
subject; this file sets the form of the answer.

Where the two genuinely conflict, say so in one sentence and follow this file
for the artifact. A `.mmd` that says what the user asked for but that
`checker.js` refuses is not a deliverable, and neither is a clean document that
models a different business — or that quietly lost half of the model it was
given.

The procedure is run the way a good partner runs **office hours**: you do the
thinking, you put real options in front of the person, you ask one question at a
time when the answer changes the next one, and you do not let them leave with
something they did not understand. The difference from a conversation is that
office hours here end in an artifact — one file — and the artifact is checked by
a machine before it leaves your hands.

**Hard gate.** Your only output is the `.mmd` and the text of your reply. Do not
write application code, scaffold a project, generate SQL migrations, or produce a
"specification document" in place of the model. The generator builds the
application from the model; your work is the model.

### 1.0 The deliverable, before anything else

**You are being asked for one file: `<business-name>.mmd`, the whole model, and
every byte of it is Mermaid.** Everything else in this protocol exists to make
that one file correct.

| Step | What it produces | Is it the deliverable? |
|---|---|---|
| §1.1 Office hours — mode, research, adversarial review, business, roster, dictionary, behaviour | Your research, your analysis and the objections you raised against both, agreed with the user | No — it is thinking, and it stays in the reply as text |
| §1.2 Write the model file | `<business-name>.mmd` | **Yes. This is the artifact.** |
| §1.3 Validate (and, for a change, prove nothing was lost) | Checker and audit reports | No — but nothing ships until they are clean |
| §1.4 Deliver | The whole file, downloadable, and what you assumed or changed | The handover |

**Three failures this protocol exists to prevent.**

1. **Prose about the model instead of the model.** Headings, bullet lists, an
   entity glossary, a lifecycle written as `draft → approved → closed` in a
   sentence, and a closing line saying "the resulting artifact is
   `orders.mmd`". That is a description of an artifact, not the artifact. Give
   the checker such a file and it answers `EML004` — *empty document: no
   entities, rules, or workflows found* — however many pages it runs to.
2. **Only the part that changed.** When you were given a model, a reply that
   says "add these lines to your `erDiagram`" is not a deliverable: the user now
   has to perform the merge by hand, in a document they did not write, which is
   exactly where an entity loses its help text and a `%%rbac` line disappears.
   You were given the whole file. Give the whole file back.
3. **A model that checks clean and is quietly smaller.** Nine entities went in
   and eight came out; every `%%report` was dropped because the rewrite went from
   memory; the help text is now a dash. The checker will not say a word — a
   smaller model is a valid model. §1.1.2 and §1.3.3 exist to catch it.

An entity is not a bullet describing a table, it is an entity block inside
`erDiagram`. A lifecycle is not an arrow in a sentence, it is a
`stateDiagram-v2`. A rule is not a paragraph, it is a `flowchart` with
`%%action` directives. A form is not a list of fields, it is `%%section` rows.

**Exactly one file leaves your hands, and it ends `.mmd`.** Not the model plus a
specification, a report, a change log, a README or a copy of the original. Where
your surface writes files, it writes one; where it attaches files, it attaches
one. Everything you want to say is text in the same reply.

**The prose failure has a signature**, and it comes back looking like progress:

```
1 auto-fix applied · 1 error
fixed   EML001   Inserted %%meta name: EML Model at line 1.
error   EML004   Empty document: no entities, rules, or workflows found.
```

`EML001` repaired plus `EML004` remaining means one thing, every time: the fixer
put a name on a document that has nothing to name. No further repair will help,
because the model was never written.

**Write the file before you write the reply.** Assemble the reply last, out of a
file that already exists and has already passed §1.3.

### 1.1 Office hours — work the business through with the user

#### 1.1.1 Decide the mode from what you were given — first, every time

**Whether this is a new model or a change is decided by one fact: did the user
give you an existing `.mmd`?** Not by their wording. "Improve my CRM" with no
file attached is a new model unless they send the file; "build me a booking app"
with a file attached is a change to that file.

| What the user gave you | Mode | Then |
|---|---|---|
| A description of a business, and no model | **New** | §1.1.3 |
| An attached or pasted `.mmd` (or a path or URL you can read), with or without a description of what to change | **Enhance** | §1.1.2 |
| A model inside a fenced block | **Enhance** | Take the block's contents verbatim as the file; strip the fence markers and nothing else |
| Several files | Ask which one is the model | Do not merge them on your own initiative |
| A request to change "my model", but no file | Ask for it, once | "Send me the `.mmd` you want changed — attach it or paste it in one fenced block." If they cannot, offer to build a new one from a description — and say that is what you are doing |
| A request to change a model you wrote earlier in this conversation | **Enhance** | Start from the exact bytes you delivered, and say so. If they have edited it since, ask for their copy — theirs is the live one |

**Never reconstruct a model from memory, from a summary, or from an earlier
draft.** A reconstruction is a new model wearing the old one's name, and every
hand-written thing in the original — help text, report SQL, a section somebody
arranged, an enum value added for one customer — is gone from it without a
single diagnostic firing. If you do not have the bytes, you do not have the
model. And **never start an enhancement from a blank document**: a model
rewritten from scratch against the same brief is the deliverable the user
explicitly did not ask for.

**Then settle the pace — ask it as the first question, together with the mode.**

> I'll **build a new model** from your description *(or: change the model you
> sent — I've read it; it has N entities)*. How do you want to work?
> 1. **Walk me through it** *(recommended)* — I propose, you correct, one decision
>    at a time, with a checked file at every gate.
> 2. **Just build it** — I work it all through myself and hand you the finished
>    file with every assumption listed.

| Pace | How the phases below run |
|---|---|
| **Walk me through it** | Every gate is a question to the user, asked with real options (a choice tool where your surface has one). A gate is a loop: present → they look → amend → re-present → approve. Offer the amend arm explicitly every time — *"tell me what to change and I'll show you again"* |
| **Just build it**, or a surface that cannot ask (a research or batch run, an API call with nobody on the other end) | Run every phase yourself, in order. Do not skip one because nobody is there to approve it — decide each gate the way a careful analyst would, and list every decision in the reply as an assumption the user can overturn |

**How to ask, when you ask.** One question at a time *when the answer changes the
next question* — who pays for this changes what you ask about billing.
Independent questions may go together. Never a numbered list of eleven questions
for the user to fill in: that is a form, and it moves the work back onto them.
**Propose, do not interrogate:** every roster, dossier and layout is presented
already filled in from domain knowledge, for the user to correct. **Never cross a
gate on inference** where the brief leaves a genuine fork — two plausible
businesses with materially different models. Fill ordinary gaps, and say which.

**If you can write files and run commands** (an agent with a workspace), keep the
session on disk so a context compaction costs nothing: a directory
`docs/eml-sessions/<business-slug>/` holding `progress.md` (the phase you are in
and each gate's decision), one dossier per entity, and the `.mmd` itself, built as
you go and checked after every edit (§1.3). On invocation, look for an unfinished
session there first and offer to resume it.

#### 1.1.2 Enhance mode — read, baseline and inventory the model first

Before you change a byte, do three things to the file exactly as it arrived.

1. **Check it.** Run the published checker over the original bytes (§1.3) and
   write the counts down. That baseline answers the question you will need later:
   was this diagnostic already there, or did you introduce it? A model that
   arrives dirty is normal. Report what you found in one line; fix what your
   change touches and every Application Dictionary gap (below); name any other
   pre-existing diagnostic you leave alone.
2. **Inventory it.** Count what it contains. This is the record §1.3.3 compares
   the result against:

   | Count | Read from |
   |---|---|
   | Entities, and their names | Every entity block in every `erDiagram` |
   | Columns per entity | The attribute lines inside each block |
   | Relationships | Every cardinality line |
   | Enums and their values; enum bindings | Every `%%enum`; every `%%field … enum:` |
   | Help text | Every `%%entity … help:` and `%%field … help:` |
   | Sections and rows | Every `%%section` |
   | Rules and actions; workflows; states and transitions; hooks; steps | `%%rule`, `%%action`, `%%workflow` (with `kind:`), each `stateDiagram-v2`, `%%hook`, `%%step` |
   | Roles, and the entities each reads | Every `%%rbac` |
   | Reports | Every `%%report` |
   | Indexes, categories, parents | Every `%%index`, `%%category`, `%%entity … parent:` |

   **Read the whole file, not the parts you think you need.** Directives sit
   beside the diagram they annotate, so a saga step writing to a column, a
   `%%section` row naming it and a `%%report` selecting it can be anywhere.
3. **Note its conventions** — naming, casing, the voice of its help text, the
   order of its sections. Your additions must read as if whoever wrote the rest
   wrote them.

Show the user the inventory in one short table, then ask what they want changed
if they have not said. Then work the change through with the same forcing
questions as a new model (§1.1.3), asked about **the change**: what is added,
what is changed, what is removed (only what they asked), what the change implies
that they did not say, which cross-entity effects it touches, and who works with
the new thing.

**Every Application Dictionary gap in the original is filled as part of this
enhancement** — an entity without help, a reference without `FK`, a status with
no enum binding, an entity whose form has no `%%section` layout. It is the one
addition you make without being asked, because nothing else in the pipeline will
ever make it, and each one is named in the delivery (§1.4).

#### 1.1.2.1 Research the domain, then attack the plan — before any question, in both modes

**Put on your thinking cap.** Everything after this point is built on what you
learn here, and a roster, a lifecycle or a rule that starts from your first
impression of a business is the commonest way for a model to check clean and be
wrong. Take the longest, most careful reasoning your surface allows, and do not
answer from the first plausible picture of the domain.

**This phase runs every time, and a `.mmd` in hand does not skip it.** In *new*
mode the brief is the subject. In *enhance* mode the subject is the business the
attached model describes plus the change asked for — do §1.1.2's check and
inventory first (they are mechanical and tell you what the model already claims),
then research the domain *around* the model. An existing model is evidence of what
someone wrote, not evidence that it is complete or right. It is also not a reason
to shorten the research: the gaps an enhancement most needs found are the ones
the original author did not think of.

**Step 1 — research as widely as you can.** Work the domain from every angle
below, using every means the surface gives you (web search and fetch, files in the
workspace, documents the user attached, the model itself) and your own knowledge
where there is no tool — and say which each finding came from. Prefer breadth
first: a finding from an angle you would otherwise have skipped is worth more than
a fifth confirmation of one you already hold.

| Angle | What you are looking for |
|---|---|
| How this kind of business actually runs | The real sequence of work from first contact to the last record, in the vocabulary its own people use |
| Who is involved | Every role, inside and outside the business, and what each does, sees and must not touch |
| What is recorded | The records, reference data and line items the work depends on, including the ones nobody mentions in a brief |
| How records change | The states each record passes through, the events between them, and the moves that are forbidden |
| The unhappy paths | Cancellations, refunds, reversals, corrections, amendments, disputes, duplicates, no-shows, late and partial everything |
| Decisions and limits | Pricing, eligibility, approval thresholds, quotas and the checks the business applies before it commits |
| Effects across records | What else must change when one thing does — stock, ledgers, availability, notifications |
| Rules from outside | Regulation, standards, contracts, retention periods and audit duties that apply *to this kind of business in the user's jurisdiction* — what must be kept, who must not see it, what must be provable |
| Established models | Industry data models, standard vocabularies and how well-known products in the space structure the same records — to borrow names and shapes, not to copy scope |
| Questions asked of the data | What each role asks at the end of the week — the source of `%%report` |
| Scale and shape | Single site or many, currencies, tax, time zones, seasonality, volumes that change a key or an index |

Keep the findings as text, one line each: the finding, its source (a URL written
in full, a document the user supplied, or *from knowledge — unverified*), and what
it implies for the model — an entity, a column, a state, a rule, a role, a report,
or *nothing; context only*. Anything you could not verify is labelled as such and
never stated as fact.

**Step 2 — turn it into a plan.** From the findings, write the working plan: the
roles, the roster (minimal and complete, §1.1.5), the lifecycles, the rules and
cross-record effects, the rules from outside, and the reports. In *enhance* mode
the plan is a gap list against the inventory — what the model lacks, what it gets
wrong, what the requested change touches — and it is a plan, not an edit. Nothing
researched enters the file yet.

**Step 3 — review the plan adversarially.** Change seats. You are no longer the
author who found these things; you are a hostile domain expert who has run this
kind of business for twenty years and has been handed your plan to tear apart.
Your job is to find what is wrong, not to confirm it. Attack at least these:

- **Evidence.** Which claims rest on one source, on marketing material, on an
  out-of-date page, on another country's rules, or on nothing but plausibility?
  What did you assume rather than find?
- **Omission.** Which role, record, state, exception, regulation or report would
  that expert say is missing? Which unhappy path has no home in the plan?
- **Excess.** Which entities, states or rules does *this* business not need?
  Scope borrowed from a larger industry standard is a cost the user pays on every
  screen.
- **Fit.** Does the plan describe the business the user actually described, or a
  more familiar neighbour of it? Which premise would the user reject on sight?
- **Consistency.** Do two findings contradict each other, or does a rule need data
  no entity in the plan records?
- **Consequence.** What does the generator make of this — a column every role can
  read that should not be, a state with no way out, a rule that acts on a column
  of another record and so never fires (§4.1)?
- **Damage** *(enhance mode)*. What in the original does the plan drop, rename,
  contradict or flatten? Which of its conventions does the plan ignore?

Write each objection down with its resolution: **accepted** (the plan changed, and
how) or **rejected** (and the evidence that answers it). A review that raised
nothing has not been done — say what you tried to break and why it held. One pass
is the floor, not the target: **run another whenever a pass changed the plan
materially**, and stop when a full pass changes nothing, not when a count runs
out.

**Step 4 — only then build, and review with the user.** What survives the review
becomes your Gate A premises (§1.1.4), the two rosters of Gate B (§1.1.5) and the
raw material of §1.1.3's seven questions; the objections you accepted are the
reason the plan looks as it does, and the user is entitled to see them.

| Pace | Where the research and the review show up |
|---|---|
| **Walk me through it** | Before Gate A, give the user a short summary: the three or four findings that most shaped the plan, the objections that changed it, and the objections that did not and why. They correct the research before they correct the roster |
| **Just build it**, or a surface that cannot ask | Do all of it yourself, and carry the findings that shaped the model, the objections you accepted and the ones you rejected into the reply as assumptions (§1.4) |

**The hard gate is unchanged.** Research and review are thinking: they stay in
the reply as text and are not a second deliverable (§1.0). If you can write
files, keep them with the session (§1.1.1) as `00-research.md` and
`01-adversarial-review.md` beside the dossiers; they are working papers, and
exactly one file — the `.mmd` — still leaves your hands. If your surface has no
means of research at all, say so in one line, work from what you know, mark every
finding *from knowledge — unverified*, and still run the review: the review needs
no tool, and it is the half that most often catches the error.

#### 1.1.3 New mode — the forcing questions

**A business description is always thinner than the model it implies.** "A
booking system for a dance studio" has not mentioned instructors, rooms,
cancellation windows, waitlists, or what happens to a class when its instructor
calls in sick — and every one of those is a table, a rule or a workflow. So, with
the research of §1.1.2.1 in hand, put the business through these seven questions.
In *walk me through it*, ask the
first one or two that the brief does not already answer, propose answers to the
rest, and let the user correct them; in *just build it*, answer all seven
yourself.

1. **Who uses it every day?** The functional roles — a salesperson, a
   dispatcher, a ward clerk — each of whom works with part of the model, not all
   of it. Every entity will belong to at least one (§6).
2. **What do they keep records of?** Every entity the business needs, not only
   the ones named — including the reference and lookup entities the described
   flow silently depends on, and the line items that have no life away from
   their owner (§3.5.1).
3. **What happens to each record over its life?** The states from creation to
   the terminal one, the event that moves it along each edge, and who may make
   each move. An entity with a `status` has a state machine whether or not
   anyone drew it; draw it (§5.2).
4. **What has to be decided or checked?** Pricing, eligibility, approval
   thresholds, limits, validation beyond types — for each, the inputs it reads
   and whether it merely **decides** or must also **act** (`%%action`, §4.2).
5. **When one thing happens, what else must happen?** Cross-entity effects —
   stock decremented by an order line, a ledger entry written by an approval, a
   slot released by a cancellation. Name the trigger, the target entity and
   whether it is a create, an update or a transition. These are the ones most
   often missed; they become hooks, rule actions or saga steps (§5.3).
6. **What does a person fill in together, on one screen?** The form layout:
   which fields are read side by side, which belong under one heading, what is
   rarely touched. This becomes `%%section` rows (§3.7) — mandatory.
7. **What do they ask of the data at the end of the week?** The questions each
   role's users actually ask, which become `%%report` directives (§7) — optional,
   but a reporting layer that answers one person's questions is half-finished.

#### 1.1.4 Premises — Gate A

Before any roster, state what you now believe in a short numbered list the user
can agree or disagree with line by line:

```
PREMISES
1. Members buy class packs; a booking spends one credit.  — agree?
2. A class with fewer than 3 bookings 12 hours before start is cancelled.  — agree?
3. Instructors are staff, not members; they never book.  — agree?
```

A premise the user rejects is the cheapest correction in the whole process. In
*just build it*, these premises are the first thing in your reply.

#### 1.1.5 The roster — Gate B, with two alternatives

Propose the entity roster as a table — entity, one-line purpose, parent (for a
line item), category, the roles that read it — and **always put two rosters in
front of the user**: the **minimal** one (the fewest entities that run the
business described) and the **complete** one (what the business will need within
a year), recommend one, and say why in one line. For an enhancement the two
alternatives are the smallest change that does what was asked and the change
done properly — the latter usually including the dictionary gaps of §1.1.2.

#### 1.1.6 The Application Dictionary, entity by entity — Gate C

**This is mandatory, and it is where the thinking goes.** The generated
application has no screen, label, lookup, dropdown, section or explanation that
the model does not declare, so every dictionary value is decided here,
deliberately, before a line of Mermaid — not improvised while the ERD is being
typed. §3.7 is the reference for every value below; read it before your first
dossier.

Write one **dossier** per entity, already filled in, and (in *walk me through
it*) walk them one at a time:

```
# Lead · standalone · category: Sales · read by: sales_rep, sales_manager
A person or company that has shown interest and has not yet been qualified …

## Fields
| Column       | Type · modifiers | Dictionary records       | Points at / enum | Help (domain knowledge, not the name)                       |
|--------------|------------------|--------------------------|------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------|
| first_name   | string           | String                   |                  | How the lead introduces themselves; used in every email.    |
| email        | email UK         | Email                    |                  | Where follow-ups go; one lead per address, or history splits.|
| status       | string           | List (LeadStatus)        | %%enum LeadStatus | Where qualification stands; only `qualified` can convert.   |
| owner_id     | string FK        | Table Direct → User      | User (person role)| The rep working the lead; reassigned when territory changes.|
| campaign_id  | string FK OPTIONAL| Table Direct → Campaign | Campaign          | The campaign that produced it; credits marketing.           |

## Form layout
Lead          — The person who showed interest and how to reach them.
                first_name | last_name
                email      | phone
                job_title
Qualification — Where the lead stands, who is working it, and how warm it is.
                status     | owner_id
                rating     | score
                lead_source| campaign_id
```

For every column decide, in the dossier and not later:

- **its type and modifiers**, and therefore the **reference type** the dictionary
  will record — the control a person gets (§3.7's table);
- **for a reference**: the entity it points at, the `FK` modifier, a name ending
  `_id` (or `_by` / a person-role name for a person) that resolves to that entity
  **by name**, and the relationship line — all four, or the dictionary records a
  text box holding a uuid;
- **for a closed vocabulary** (status, state, stage, type, priority, tier …): the
  `%%enum` and the `%%field … enum:` binding;
- **its help**: what the value means in this business, where it comes from, and
  what depends on it — the sentence a new employee needs;
- **its place on the form**: the `%%section` and the row, beside the column it
  is filled in with.

And for every entity: its `%%entity … help:`, its `%%category` (with `name:`),
whether it is a line item (`parent:`), the column that will name it in every
lookup (§3.7, display value), and its **form layout** — headed sections, two
fields per row, every column but the key placed exactly once (§3.7, *Form
layout*). An entity whose layout you have not decided is an entity whose dossier
is not finished.

#### 1.1.7 Behaviour — Gate D

Last, the cross-cutting pass, over the agreed dossiers: the state machine for
every lifecycle column (§5.2), the rules and their actions (§4), the hooks and
sagas for every cross-entity effect (§5.1, §5.3) — for a write to another
entity, which of its rows the step aims at (`targetSource` or `targetField`,
else `EML265`) — one `%%rbac … .read` line per entity and the restrictions on
writes and transitions (§6), and the `%%report` questions per role (§7). Present
it as one table per kind; in *walk me through it*, this is the last gate before
the file is finished.

What none of this may do is stop the work. A question raised instead of a file
leaves the user with nothing to correct; a question raised beside a file they
can already run costs them one sentence to answer.

### 1.2 Write the model file

Now write the document, following §2 to §7 in full. Every entity from the roster
appears; every column from its dossier, with its type, modifiers, binding and
help; every form layout as `%%section` lines; every rule as a `%%rule` flowchart
or an `%%action`; every cross-entity effect as a hook, an action or a step;
every multi-step flow as a saga. Nothing you agreed in §1.1 is allowed to survive
only as prose.

**Every Application Dictionary value is mandatory, and all of them are filled in
the `.mmd`.** Nine checker codes mean a dictionary value is missing, and the
audit fails a model that carries any of them. None is advisory, whatever the
severity of the warning says:

| Code | The value that is missing |
|---|---|
| `EML119` | the `FK` modifier on a reference column (`_id` / `_by` resolving to an entity) — without it the lookup is lost |
| `EML146` | the `%%field … enum:` binding on a status, state or stage column — without it the dropdown is lost |
| `EML151` | help that describes its subject rather than restating its name |
| `EML152` | `%%entity <Name> help:` on an entity |
| `EML153` | `%%field <Entity>.<column> help:` on every column but the primary key |
| `EML154` | `name:` on a `%%category` — without it the grouping is dropped |
| `EML170` | `%%section` on an entity — without it the form is one flat, unheaded column of fields |
| `EML172` | a `%%section` row for every column but the key — an unplaced column falls into a trailing `Other` section |
| `EML177` | `help:` on a `%%section`, saying what that part of the form is for |

The delivered file carries none of these nine. Not "a few", not "only on the
obvious columns": none.

**The file contract.** Every line of it is checkable in seconds, so check it:

| | |
|---|---|
| **Name** | `<business-name>.mmd` — lower-case, hyphenated, no spaces: `acme-dance-studio.mmd`. An enhanced model keeps the name it arrived with |
| **Count** | Exactly one file — this one. Not one per entity, not an ERD file plus a rules file, and no companion `.md`, report, README or archive |
| **Encoding** | UTF-8 plain text |
| **First non-blank line** | A `%%` line. A comment banner naming the business is fine; `%%meta name:` must appear before the first Mermaid keyword |
| **Every other line** | A Mermaid statement, an EML `%%` directive, or blank |
| **Never in the file** | Markdown headings, bullets, tables, bold, prose paragraphs, triple-backtick fences, YAML front matter, JSON wrappers, HTML comments |
| **Anything you want to say** | Goes in the reply, or in a `%%` comment line inside the file |

The document runs top to bottom in this order — the ERD first, its directives
beside it, then each rules and workflow section opened by its own `%%meta`:

```
%%meta name: <Business Name>          <- before the first section keyword
%%meta kind: erd
%%meta version: 1.0.0

%%enum <StatusName>: a, b, c          <- one per closed vocabulary
erDiagram
    <Entity> {
        string id PK
        ...
    }
    <Entity> ||--o{ <Other> : "verb"   <- every relationship, with a real verb
%%field <Entity>.status enum: <StatusName>
%%entity <Entity> help: <what it is for in this business>
%%field <Entity>.<column> help: <what the value means here>
%%section entity: <Entity>; name: <Heading>; help: <what this part is for>; rows: <a>, <b> | <c>
%%index <Entity>(<column>)

%%meta name: <Rule Name>              <- a new section starts at its own %%meta
%%meta kind: rules
%%rule <ruleName> on <Entity> event: beforeCreate priority: 10
flowchart TD
    ...
    %%action <name> validation-error when: <expr> message: ...

%%meta name: <Lifecycle Name>
%%meta kind: workflow
%%workflow <Name> entity: <Entity> kind: state
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> <first>
    ...
    <last> --> [*]
    %%rbac role:<role> on <Entity>.<transition>
```

§9 is that skeleton filled in — a complete, checker-clean document with every
construct in it. It is the shape of what you deliver; imitate it.

**Enhance mode adds the preservation rules.** Work from the original bytes, in
the original order, and keep everything you were not asked to change. None of
these is reported by the checker:

| Rule | What breaks when it is ignored |
|---|---|
| **Keep every line you were not asked to change** | The rewrite-from-memory failure: anything the original had and yours does not is a silent loss |
| **Keep the document's order** | Reordering turns a two-line change into an unreviewable diff |
| **Never rename anything silently** | An entity name is a foreign-key prefix, an `%%rbac` target, a rule binding, a `%%section entity:`, and a table name in every `%%report` — all must move together |
| **Never drop help text, a section, or a `%%report`** | They are the application's explanation, its forms and its users' questions, and nothing complains when they go |
| **Never narrow an enum a state machine uses** | Every state bound to the missing value becomes unreachable; the diagram still draws |
| **Add, do not replace, unless asked** | "Also track X" means the model gains X, not that it becomes X |

**And follow the blast radius of every change:**

| When you… | Also update |
|---|---|
| Add an entity | Its relationships at both ends; `%%rbac … .read` for every role that works with it; help on it and every column; enums and bindings; its `%%section` layout; a `%%category`; `parent:` if it is a line item |
| Add a column | Type and modifiers; help; enum binding; the `FK` modifier **and** a relationship line if it points at another entity; **a place in a `%%section` row**; any `%%report` that should select it |
| Add a state | The enum behind the status column gains the value; entries and exits still reach `[*]`; any `%%rbac` on the new transition |
| Add a role | One `%%rbac … .read` per entity that role works with |
| Rename or remove anything | Every reference to it: foreign-key prefixes, relationships, `%%rbac`, `%%rule`, `%%workflow`, `%%hook`, `%%step`, `%%field`, `%%section`, `%%index`, and the SQL inside every `%%report` |

Keep `%%meta name:` unless asked to rename the business, and raise
`%%meta version:` if the document carries one.

Every EML document is valid Mermaid (§0), so the finished file must render in a
Mermaid viewer as well as compile. A viewer that refuses the file is telling you
the bytes are not what you think they are. To see all of it — the rules,
workflows, roles and forms Mermaid treats as comments — open it in the model
viewer at `https://www.appwithai.org/viewers/`.

Check a directive's `status` (§7) before relying on it. `%%rule` and `%%trigger`
are validated but not compiled — do not promise the user behaviour that rides on
them.

### 1.3 Validate — check, fix, audit, and review until clean

The model is not finished when it is written. It is finished when the checker
accepts it, the audit scores it complete, and — for a change — the inventory says
nothing was lost. The two modules and their API are in §8.

#### 1.3.1 The checker and the fixer

**If you have a shell, this is the whole step** — any runtime with Node 18+, Bun
or Deno, nothing to install:

```sh
curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/check-model.mjs
node check-model.mjs my-business.mmd
```

It runs the three passes below against the published modules, prints the
checker's own report, and exits `0` when the model is clean, `1` when the
generator would refuse it, `2` when the runner could not run at all. (`--write` saves the repairs it applied; §8.4 has the
rest, and the recipes for runtimes with no shell.) Written out:

```js
import { check, formatReport } from "https://www.appwithai.org/guide/checker.js";
import { checkAndFix }          from "https://www.appwithai.org/guide/fixer.js";

let model = /* the exact bytes of the .mmd you just wrote */;

// Pass 1 — repair the auto-fixable codes, then re-check what survived.
let report = checkAndFix(model);
model = report.source;

// Passes 2 and 3 — check the repaired bytes, and confirm they are stable.
for (let pass = 2; pass <= 3 && report.ok; pass++) {
  report = { ...check(model), source: model };
}
```

**Validate the file, not your message.** `check()` takes the contents of the
`.mmd` and nothing else. If the repairs change anything, the file you hand over
is `report.source`, not the draft you started from.

**`EML004` means you fed it something that is not a model** — specification
prose, an empty file, a path instead of its contents. Go back to §1.2.

**Iterate until clean — at least 10 cycles.** Run the checker, fix every
diagnostic (the fixer for the auto-fixable codes, you for the rest), re-run.
Repeat **at least 10 times or until the checker reports zero errors and zero
warnings**, whichever comes first. A repair can uncover a problem the original
error was masking, so a single clean pass immediately after an edit describes a
document that no longer exists. Read each diagnostic's `code`, `line`, the text
of that line, and its `hint`; fix the cause in the model, not the symptom in the
text. If diagnostics persist after 10 cycles, deliver the best version, say
plainly which remain and what you tried. In *walk me through it*, run this loop
after **every** edit to the file, not only at the end — no gate closes over a
document with errors.

**The fixer repairs layout mechanics, not layout design.** `EML172` (columns no
row places) is auto-fixable: the fixer appends them to the entity's last section,
two per row. That keeps the field on the form; it does not put it where it
belongs. Move it.

#### 1.3.2 The audit — is the model finished?

A clean report is not a finished model: one entity with a key and a name is
valid EML. Run the second published runner, which scores §10's checklist:

```sh
curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/audit-model.mjs
node audit-model.mjs my-business.mmd
```

Its last line must read `23 passed, 0 failed`. A model that fails it is not
delivered as finished (§8.5).

#### 1.3.3 Enhance mode — prove nothing was lost

Put the §1.1.2 inventory beside the same counts taken from the enhanced file.
Every number must have gone **up, or stayed the same** — unless the user asked
for it to go down:

| If this fell and nobody asked | You have |
|---|---|
| Entity count, or an entity name vanished | Dropped an entity |
| Columns on an entity you did not touch | Rewritten it from memory |
| Enum values | Broken every state and rule bound to the missing one |
| Help lines | Emptied the generated manual |
| `%%section` lines or rows | Flattened a form somebody designed |
| `%%rbac` lines | Made an entity invisible to a role that could see it yesterday |
| `%%report` directives | Deleted a question somebody's users ask |
| Hooks, rules, actions, steps, workflows | Removed behaviour the application was running |

A fall the user did not request is a defect, not a simplification. Put it back,
and validate again from zero.

#### 1.3.4 Review until the model is perfect, not until a count runs out

A clean run starts the review; it does not end it. After every clean run:

1. Re-read the file against the dossiers, entity by entity and column by column:
   every value decided in §1.1 is in the file, as decided.
2. Confirm none of the nine dictionary codes (§1.2), and the audit's
   `23 passed, 0 failed`.
3. Read every help line and every section heading as the person using the
   generated screen would. Rewrite any line that would not tell a new employee
   something true about this business, and any section that groups fields by
   kind (*Dates*, *References*) rather than by what the person is doing.
4. If anything was found, fix it, run the checker and the audit again **from
   zero**, and review again.

Repeat until a full review finds nothing to change.

#### 1.3.5 If you cannot reach the checker

That changes what you can *claim*, not whether you tried: validation is mandatory,
so this section is the last step of a failed search, never a first step. First make sure it is
actually true: §8.4 lists a route per runtime, and every observed case of "the
checker could not be run" has been one route failing while the others went
untried. Failing to reach GitHub says nothing about whether the checker can
run — no route to it passes through a GitHub host. A host that will not resolve,
or a proxy answering 403 or 502, is one route — the modules are two dependency-free files, and `check-model.mjs` runs
against a local copy of them with no network at all (§8.4). Only when that is
also impossible — and you have read `check-model-standalone.mjs` and run it, or asked the user to run the
model in their own browser at `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/11-check-a-model.html`, where the **Check**
and **Audit** buttons run the same two modules — walk §10 by hand, item by item, and hand
over the file labelled **not validated**, with one plain sentence: the checker and the audit could not be run
here, this is what was verified by hand, and no counts are given. The `.mmd` is still the deliverable. Never
report a check of your own devising in the vocabulary of the real one, and never state a count, a verdict or a
score that a run did not print.

§10 asks whether the model is *right*. This table is the other half — the
mechanical faults the checker catches by reading, which a human eye slides past:

| Read your file and confirm | Code it prevents |
|---|---|
| There is an `erDiagram` with at least one entity block | `EML004` |
| `%%meta name:` is present | `EML001` |
| Every entity declares exactly one `PK` | `EML117` |
| Every foreign key column ends `_id` | `EML114` |
| Every foreign key's prefix resolves to a declared entity **by name** — `purchase_order_line_id` finds `PurchaseOrderLine`, and nothing if the entity is called `POLine` | `EML502` |
| Every foreign key has a matching relationship line | `EML502` |
| Every modifier is one of `PK` `FK` `UK` `UNIQUE` `OPTIONAL` `NULL` | `EML118` |
| Every type appears in the §3.2 table | `EML115` |
| Every `%%field … enum:` names a declared `%%enum` | `EML501` |
| Every `%%section` names a declared entity, its own columns, and at most two per row | `EML173` `EML176` `EML174` |
| Every state machine has `[*] --> <first>` and `<last> --> [*]` | `EML421` `EML422` |
| Every state is a value of the enum bound to that status column | `EML426` `EML428` |
| Every `%%rbac` / `%%rule` / `%%workflow` / `%%hook` / `%%step` names a declared entity | `EML213` `EML251` `EML242` `EML202` `EML266` |
| Every `%%rbac` target is a CRUD operation or a transition that machine declares | `EML214` |
| Every `kind: saga` marked `trigger: rule` is named by some `%%action` | `EML286` |
| Every `%%rule` is bound with `on <Entity> event: <hookType>` | `EML506` |
| Every Update or Delete step on another entity says which row — `targetSource` or `targetField` | `EML265` |

### 1.4 Deliver

**Run the loop one last time, over the exact bytes you are about to hand over.**
Editing stops; validation starts again from zero. The file that leaves your hands
is the one that came out of a clean run — not an earlier draft, not "clean three
edits ago".

Hand back the **whole** `<business-name>.mmd` as **a file the user can
download**, not something they must reconstruct out of a chat log.

- If you can write to a filesystem, write it there under that exact name and
  attach it.
- If your surface has a file, download or artifact mechanism, use it, with the
  `.mmd` extension intact — not `.txt`, not `.md`, not `.diff`.
- **Only if the surface truly cannot carry a file**: print the document inside a
  single triple-backtick `mermaid` fence, the file name on the line above it, the
  file's bytes and nothing else between the fences, and nothing left out. No
  elisions, no "unchanged from above", no "the rest of your model as before".
- **If your surface only ever produces a document** — a research report, a
  canvas, one long answer — that document *opens* with the model: the file name,
  then the single fenced block, then one line telling the reader to save it as
  `<business-name>.mmd`. Your prose goes after it.
- **Do not offer the by-products** — an outline, a draft, a diff, a change log as
  a file. One attachment.

Alongside the file — in the reply, never inside it — give:

| | New | Enhance |
|---|---|---|
| **What you understood** | The premises and the roster, so the user can correct what you guessed | What changed: added, changed, removed, and what you inferred rather than were told |
| **What the research and the review found** | The findings that shaped the model, the adversarial objections you accepted and the ones you rejected (§1.1.2.1) | The same, plus the gaps you found in the original and what you did about each |
| **What was preserved** | — | The inventory table, before and after, side by side (§1.3.3) |
| **The checker result** | Errors, warnings and infos, with counts | The same, for the model as received *and* as delivered |
| **The dictionary** | Zero of the nine codes, and the audit's last line | The same, plus every dictionary gap of the original you filled — sections included |
| **What is open** | Assumptions and unresolved forks | Assumptions, forks, and any pre-existing diagnostic you left alone |
| **What to do next** | Upload the file at `https://www.appwithai.org/guide/run-in-browser.html#upload`, where it becomes a running application in the browser tab, or open it in `https://www.appwithai.org/viewers/` to see every rule, workflow and form | Same |

**Completion status** — say which, in one line at the end:

- **DONE** — checker clean, audit `23 passed, 0 failed`, every gate approved (or,
  in *just build it*, every decision listed).
- **DONE WITH CONCERNS** — delivered, with the open questions listed.
- **NEEDS CONTEXT** — the user left a fork unanswered that changes the model;
  delivered on the recommended reading, and the fork named.

One last check before you send. Open the file you are about to attach and read
its first non-blank line. If it does not begin with `%%`, you are attaching the
wrong artifact. If you were given a model, count its entities: a count lower than
the one you wrote down in §1.1.2 is a regression.

---

## 2. Document structure

A document is UTF-8 text holding one or more **sections**. A section opens at a
Mermaid keyword and runs to the next one.

| Opening keyword | Section |
|---|---|
| `erDiagram` | ERD |
| `flowchart` / `graph` | business rules **or** workflow |
| `stateDiagram-v2` | workflow (state-machine form) |

A `flowchart` is read as **rules** when preceded by `%%meta kind: rules`, or when
it contains only decision/expression/function/io shapes and no `%%hook`
directives. Otherwise it is a **workflow**. Say which you mean — mark every rules
section `%%meta kind: rules` rather than relying on inference.

Directives are Mermaid comments and may sit inside or beside their section:

```
%%meta name: Acme Dance Studio
%%meta kind: erd
%%meta version: 1.0.0
```

`%%meta name:` is required — its absence is `EML001`, one of the five codes the
fixer repairs. Give the document a real business name rather than letting the
fixer guess one from the first entity.

A minimal, complete, checker-clean document:

```mermaid
%%meta name: Minimal Example
%%meta kind: erd
erDiagram
    Customer {
        string id PK
        string email UK
        string name
    }

%%entity Customer help: A person or organisation that buys from us. Created when a lead converts, and never deleted while an unpaid invoice stands against it.
%%field Customer.email help: The address invoices and order confirmations are sent to, and the customer's identity here. Unique, because two records on one address split a customer's history in two.
%%field Customer.name help: The trading name to address on correspondence and to print on an invoice. Not necessarily the registered legal entity.
%%section entity: Customer; name: Customer; help: Who is buying, under the name and address every invoice carries.; rows: name, email
```

---

## 3. The ERD section

### 3.1 Entities and attributes

```mermaid
%%meta name: Studio Booking
%%meta kind: erd

%%enum ClassStatus: scheduled, running, completed, cancelled

erDiagram
    Instructor {
        string id PK
        string full_name
        string email UK
        boolean is_active
    }
    Room {
        string id PK
        string name
        integer capacity
    }
    DanceClass {
        string id PK
        string instructor_id FK
        string room_id FK
        string title
        string status
        datetime starts_at
        integer capacity
        decimal price OPTIONAL
    }
    Instructor ||--o{ DanceClass : "teaches"
    Room ||--o{ DanceClass : "hosts"

%%field DanceClass.status enum: ClassStatus
%%index DanceClass(instructor_id, starts_at)

%%entity Instructor help: Somebody who teaches at the studio. Instructors are booked against classes, so deactivating one has to leave their past classes attributed rather than delete them.
%%field Instructor.full_name help: The name that appears on the timetable, which is how members choose a class. Use the name the studio advertises, not the one on the contract.
%%field Instructor.email help: Where the schedule and cancellation notices are sent, and how the instructor signs in. Unique, because it identifies the person.
%%field Instructor.is_active help: Whether the instructor is currently teaching. Cleared instead of deleting, so the timetable history and the members' attendance records stay intact.

%%entity Room help: A physical studio a class can be held in. Rooms are the constraint the timetable is built against: two classes cannot share one, and capacity is what caps a class's bookings.
%%field Room.name help: What the room is called on the timetable and on the door. Members navigate by it, so keep it the name actually painted on the wall.
%%field Room.capacity help: The most people the room legally holds, including the instructor. It is the ceiling on a class's own capacity, and it is a fire regulation rather than a preference.

%%entity DanceClass help: One session at one time in one room with one instructor. The class is what a member books onto and what the studio is paid for, and its status is the single answer to whether it is going ahead.
%%field DanceClass.instructor_id help: Who is teaching this session. Changing it is a substitution, and members who booked for a named instructor generally want to be told.
%%field DanceClass.room_id help: Where the session is held. It caps the class's capacity and is what a member is looking for when they arrive.
%%field DanceClass.title help: What the class is called on the timetable — the style and level a member is choosing between. "Beginners' salsa", not "Class 14".
%%field DanceClass.status help: scheduled — open for bookings; running — under way; completed — taught, and countable in attendance; cancelled — called off, and every booking on it has to be refunded or moved.
%%field DanceClass.starts_at help: When the session begins, in the studio's own time zone. It is what the timetable is ordered by and what a reminder is sent against.
%%field DanceClass.capacity help: The most bookings this session will take, at or below the room's own limit. Set lower than the room where the style needs floor space.
%%field DanceClass.price help: What a member pays for this session if they are not using a class pack. Empty where the class is included in a membership.
%%section entity: Instructor; name: Instructor; help: Who teaches, how the studio reaches them, and whether they can be timetabled.; rows: full_name, email | is_active
%%section entity: Room; name: Room; help: The studio room and how many dancers it safely holds.; rows: name, capacity
%%section entity: DanceClass; name: Class; help: What is taught, by whom, where, and whether it is going ahead.; rows: title, status | instructor_id, room_id
%%section entity: DanceClass; name: Session; help: When it runs, how many it takes, and what a drop-in pays.; rows: starts_at, capacity | price
```

One entity block per entity. One attribute per line: `<type> <name> [MODIFIERS]`.
Entity names are `PascalCase` or `SNAKE_CASE`; attribute names are `snake_case`.

`id PK` is added automatically when an entity declares no primary key, but
declaring one yourself is better — `EML117` warns when you do not, and the repair
prepends `string id PK`, which may not be the column you wanted.

**Seven column names are the generator's — do not declare them.** Every
generated table carries them already, in both stacks:

```
id  version  created_at  updated_at  created_by  updated_by  deleted_at  deleted_by
```

Writing `datetime created_at` in an entity block says something the generator
already guarantees. `EML103` reports the line, `checkAndFix` deletes it (§8.3),
and the generator keeps its own definition regardless. Until it learned to, the duplicate reached
PostgreSQL as a `CREATE TABLE` naming one column twice — which is rejected
outright, so the *application failed to open*, with a message
(`column "created_at" specified more than once`) that named no model line at
all. Model what your business knows; the record-keeping columns are already
there.

The `_id` spelling is a different column and a legitimate one:
`created_by` is the generator's audit stamp — a bare UUID with no lookup —
while `created_by_id FK` is a reference you modelled, and it resolves to your
model's person entity with a lookup on it (§3.5). If you want the author of a record to
be selectable and shown by name, declare `created_by_id FK`, not `created_by`.

### 3.2 Types

Eight canonical types. Everything else normalises into one of them; an unknown
type falls back to `string` and raises `EML115`.

| Canonical | Written as any of |
|---|---|
| `string` | `string` `varchar` `char` `uuid` `guid` `id` `email` `url` `phone` `password` `color` |
| `text` | `text` `longtext` |
| `integer` | `integer` `int` `bigint` `smallint` |
| `decimal` | `decimal` `float` `double` `number` `money` `amount` |
| `boolean` | `boolean` `bool` |
| `date` | `date` |
| `datetime` | `datetime` `timestamp` `time` |
| `json` | `json` `jsonb` `object` `array` |

The alias you choose is not cosmetic even though it normalises: `email`, `phone`,
`url`, `password` and `color` all become `string` in SQL, and the word you wrote
is kept — it is what the Application Dictionary records as the column's reference
type, and therefore what decides the control the user gets (§3.7). Write
`email email`, `phone mobile`, `url website`, `password secret` and
`color brand_colour`; a column declared `string` gets a plain text box even when
its name says otherwise. Prefer the specific alias over the canonical name
wherever one fits.

### 3.3 Modifiers

| Modifier | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `PK` | Primary key. Implies unique. |
| `FK` | Foreign key. Marks the column as a reference. |
| `UK` / `UNIQUE` | Unique. |
| `OPTIONAL` / `NULL` | Nullable. |

**Defaults**: every column is *required* unless marked `OPTIONAL` or `NULL` (or
it is the `PK`), and *not unique* unless marked `UK`, `UNIQUE` or `PK`.

Anything that is not one of these six words is **dropped silently** by the parser
— `string email UNQIUE` yields a column that is simply not unique and renders
identically in the diagram. `EML118` warns about it. Read that warning.

### 3.4 Relationships and cardinality

Mermaid's ER grammar lets you pair any left marker with any right marker. **EML
reads these eight spellings, and only these eight:**

| Operator | Kind | Example |
|---|---|---|
| `\|\|--\|\|` | one to one | `User \|\|--\|\| Profile : has` |
| `\|o--o\|` | one to one | `Employee \|o--o\| ParkingSpot : assigned` |
| `\|\|--o{` | one to many | `Company \|\|--o{ Contact : employs` |
| `\|\|--\|{` | one to many | `Order \|\|--\|{ OrderItem : contains` |
| `}o--\|\|` | many to one | `Deal }o--\|\| DealStage : in_stage` |
| `}\|--\|\|` | many to one | `OrderItem }\|--\|\| Order : belongs_to` |
| `}o--o{` | many to many | `Student }o--o{ Course : enrolls` |
| `}\|--\|{` | many to many | `Author }\|--\|{ Book : writes` |

**A relationship spelled any other way is dropped in silence.** `Appointment
||--o| Consultation : "becomes"` is valid Mermaid and renders exactly as drawn,
but no relationship reaches the model — and nothing points at the line. What you
get instead is `EML502` on a foreign key whose parent "has no relationship", or
`EML503` on an entity that now looks isolated. When a diagnostic denies a
relationship you know you drew, check its operator against the eight above before
anything else. Optional-on-the-many-side is `||--o{`; optional one-to-one is
`|o--o|`; there is no eight-operator spelling for "exactly zero or one child", so
model it as one-to-many and let the rule enforce the rest.

The label after the colon is the verb of the relationship and appears in the
generated interface. Write a real one — `"places"`, `"employs"`, `"hosts"` — not
`"has"` repeated.

### 3.5 Foreign keys

A foreign key resolves **by name**: a column ending `_id` points at the entity
whose snake_case name it carries. `customer_id` finds `Customer`;
`sla_policy_id` finds `SlaPolicy`.

- A foreign key that does not end `_id` cannot be resolved: `EML114`, and the
  fixer appends the suffix.
- **The prefix has to match the entity's name as the parser derives it.**
  `purchase_order_line_id` finds `PurchaseOrderLine`. It does not find `POLine`,
  because `po_line` reads back as `PoLine` — an entity whose name runs two
  capitals together cannot be reached by a foreign key. Name such an entity
  `PurchaseOrderLine` rather than trying to spell the column around it.
- **Columns naming a person resolve to the model's person entity, but only by an
  exact list.** Anything ending `_by` or `_by_id` — `created_by_id`,
  `approved_by_id`, `received_by_id` — plus these names: `assigned_to`,
  `author_id`, `lab_manager_id`, `manager_id`, `owner_id`, `pi_id`,
  `remediation_owner`, `remediation_owner_id`, `user_id`. Nothing else.
  `approver_id` derives `Approver` and `assigned_to_id` derives `AssignedTo` —
  entities nobody declared. Name person columns `<verb>_by_id`
  (`approved_by_id`) or use `owner_id`.
- **A name that resolves to nothing falls back to a relationship you drew.** If
  the entity declares a parent that no other foreign key on it accounts for, the
  column is bound to that parent — so `ImagingReport.radiologist_id` finds
  `Doctor` when the model says `Doctor ||--o{ ImagingReport`, rather than
  hunting for a `Radiologist` nobody wrote. The generator resolves it this way,
  and the checker agrees rather than reporting a column that in fact works.
  `EML502` remains for the case with nothing to fall back on: a foreign key
  whose name matches no entity *and* whose entity declares no spare parent.
  Relying on the fallback is still worse than naming the column well — it is
  unambiguous only while the entity has exactly one unclaimed parent.
- **Which entity that is, is read off your model.** `User` if you declared one,
  otherwise `Staff`, otherwise `Employee` — the first of the three that exists.
  So `pi_id` in a research model with a `User` entity resolves to `User`, and
  `reported_by_id` in a hospital model that has `Staff` and no `User` resolves to
  `Staff` rather than raising `EML502` for a `User` entity you never wrote. A
  model with none of the three still resolves to `User`, which is the diagnostic
  you want: declare a person entity, or the reference has nothing to point at.
- **Two names on that list are traps**: `assigned_to` and `remediation_owner` are
  recognised, but they do not end `_id`, so they raise `EML114` — and the repair
  renames them to `assigned_to_id` and `remediation_owner_id`, which are *not* on
  the list, so `EML502` appears where a warning was cleared. It is the one repair
  that can leave a new diagnostic behind. Do not use those two names; write
  `owner_id`.
- Declare the matching relationship line as well as the column. A `FK` with no
  relationship raises `EML502`, and the generated interface loses the navigation
  the relationship would have given it.

### 3.5.1 Parent and child — line items

Some entities have no life away from their owner: an invoice line, an order
line, a prescription item. **The ERD cannot express this**, which is the whole
reason the directive exists — `InvoiceLine.invoice_id` and `Invoice.patient_id`
are both a foreign key with a relationship behind it, and nothing in Mermaid
says that a line means nothing without its invoice while a patient means a great
deal without one.

```
%%entity InvoiceLine parent: Invoice
```

**Decide it with these questions, in this order:**

1. Would a list of these records, *away from their owner*, be useful to anyone?
   A screen of every invoice line ever written is not a screen anyone opens. If
   no — it is a child.
2. Does the row's identity depend on the owner? "Line 1 of invoice 7", not
   "line 1". If yes — it is a child.
3. Would deleting the owner make the row meaningless? If yes — it is a child.

A **reference** is the opposite on all three: `Invoice.patient_id` points at a
Patient who exists, and matters, on their own. Most foreign keys are references.
Line items are the minority, and they are usually obvious once the questions are
asked — the noun is a *line*, an *item*, a *detail*, an *entry*.

**What it does to the application:**

| | Parent | Child |
|---|---|---|
| `sys_window` | its own | **none** |
| Dashboard | a card | **no card — not navigable** |
| `sys_tab` | `tab_level: 0` | `tab_level: 1`, in the *parent's* window |
| Reached by | opening the window | opening a parent record |

The tab links on the child's own foreign key back to the parent — the one
already in the ERD, marked `sys_column.is_parent` and stored as
`sys_tab.link_column_id`. **Do not declare a second column for it**, and do not
drop the relationship line: the directive names the parent, the ERD still draws
the edge.

Four codes police it:

| Code | Severity | Fires when |
|---|---|---|
| `EML147` | error | the parent is not declared, or an entity names itself |
| `EML148` | error | the child has no foreign key back — nothing for the tab to link on |
| `EML149` | info | an entity is *shaped* like a line item and declares no `parent:` |
| `EML150` | warning | a declared child is still named in a `%%category` |

`EML147` and `EML148` are errors because a line item with nothing to link on
loses its own window and gains no tab, which is an entity that has quietly left
the application.

`EML149` is an **info and never an error**, because the three questions above are
about the business and not about the document: only you know whether a list of
these records away from their owner is a screen anyone opens. The checker can
only say that the shape is there, and it names both the candidate parent and the
column a tab would link on. It fires on two shapes, each of which also requires
that foreign key: an entity whose name **begins** with a declared entity's name
(`InvoiceLine`/`Invoice`, `TeamMember`/`Team`,
`FinancialPlanAssumption`/`FinancialPlan`), and an entity whose name **ends** in a
line-item noun — `Line`, `LineItem`, `Item`, `Detail`, `Entry`, `Row` — whose
foreign key resolves to a declared entity (`RecommendationItem` under
`InvestmentRecommendation`).

**Answer every `EML149` before you deliver.** Either declare the parent, or
satisfy yourself that the entity is a thing in its own right and leave it — an
`EML149` you have walked and rejected is not a fault, and the run still reports
`OK`. What is not acceptable is not having looked: if nobody decides, the default
is a dashboard card listing every line ever written and a parent record that does
not show its own lines.

`EML150` is a warning rather than an error because nothing breaks — but the two
directives contradict each other. `parent:` takes the child's dashboard card
away and the category asks for one, so the group counts an entity the reader can
never open from it. Take the child out of the `entities:` list.

**What the running application does with it.** Both stacks read the same three
rows and nothing else. Opening a parent record shows one tab per line item below
the form, each listing only the rows whose `is_parent` column holds that
record's key, with a live count on the tab and a row click that opens the child.
The dashboard and the navigation are built from the entities that have a window,
so the child appears in neither. None of that is decided by a screen — it is
`sys_tab.tab_level`, `sys_tab.link_column_id` and `sys_column.is_parent`, which
is why the model's answer and the application's arrangement cannot drift apart.

A child is still a real table with real rules, access control and a form. Only
its *placement* changes. Leave it out of `%%category`: a category lists what
appears on the dashboard, and a child does not.

### 3.6 Enums, field metadata, indexes and grouping

```
%%enum LeadStatus: new, working, qualified, converted, disqualified
%%field Lead.status enum: LeadStatus
%%field Lead.score help: 0-100, set by the scoring rule. Anything over 70 routes to a salesperson.
%%entity Lead help: Someone who has shown interest but is not yet an account.
%%index Lead(campaign_id, status)
%%index Contact(email) unique
%%category name: Sales; description: Leads and the deals they become; icon: TrendingUp; color: #0ea5e9; entities: Lead, Opportunity
```

- **`%%enum`** declares a closed vocabulary. Reference it from a column with
  `%%field`, and from a state machine's states (§5.2).
- **`%%field <E>.<attr> enum: <Name>`** binds a column to an enum. The enum must
  exist — `EML501` otherwise.
- **`%%field <E>.<attr> help: <sentence>`** is the help text for the column. It
  becomes `sys_column.description`, which the generated form prints under the
  control and the Application Dictionary shows beside the column. `enum:` and
  `help:` are the two `%%field` keys that compile; the others (`ui`, `default`,
  `min`, `max`, `format`) are accepted and validated only.
- **`%%entity <Name> help: <sentence>`** — or `description:`, the same key — is
  the sentence that explains the entity. It becomes `sys_table.description`.

**Help is not optional. Write `%%entity <Name> help:` for every entity and
`%%field <Entity>.<column> help:` for every column, without exception.**

This is the most-skipped part of a model and the most expensive to skip. The
generated application has no other source of explanation: no tooltips written by
hand, no README beside the form, no designer to ask. What you write here is what
a user reads under the control, what the Application Dictionary shows beside the
column, and the whole of the manual the generator ships. Leave it out and the
application still runs — which is exactly why it gets left out — but every field
on every form is a label with nothing behind it.

- **Every entity**, including the self-evident ones. "Invoice" is not a
  description of an invoice.
- **Every column**, including `status`, the foreign keys and the enums. A
  reference column should say what the reference is *for* — "the ward this bed
  stands in" — not restate its type.
- **Say what it is for, not what it is.** `%%field Lead.score help: 0-100, set by
  the scoring rule. Anything over 70 routes to a salesperson.` tells a reader
  something. `The score of the lead.` does not.
- **Nobody adds it later.** The model is the only place it can be written, and
  the moment it is being written is the only moment anyone knows the answer.

**And it has to be domain knowledge, not the name in a sentence.** This is where
the *business* lands in the model, and nothing else in the document carries it.
The ERD says an entity has a `household_id`; only help says that a membership
belongs to a family and that the family's screen is where it is read. Everything
else — types, keys, cardinalities, states, roles — is structure, and structure
is the half a reader can already see. Help is the half that has to be *known*:
what the business calls this, why it keeps it, what depends on it, what goes
wrong when it is wrong. Write it from the research and the brief, in the
business's own vocabulary.

**One test, applied to every line before you deliver: could this sentence have
been written without knowing anything about this business?** If yes, it is not
help.

```
Bad:   %%field HouseholdMember.household_id help: Household id for HouseholdMember.
Good:  %%field HouseholdMember.household_id help: The family this membership is in. Listed inside the household's own screen — a membership away from its household is not something anybody looks up.

Bad:   %%entity Address help: Address is a business record in the platform.
Good:  %%entity Address help: A postal address belonging to a party, kept as its own record because a party has several — registered, correspondence, often an overseas one — and because a change of address is a KYC event that has to be evidenced rather than typed over the old one.
```

The first of each pair would pass any coverage check and leaves the reader
exactly where they started.

**Three codes report the three ways a model fails here, all warnings:**

| Code | Fires when |
|---|---|
| `EML152` | an entity carries no `%%entity … help:` at all |
| `EML153` | an entity has columns with no `%%field … help:` — reported once per entity, naming them |
| `EML151` | help that restates its own subject instead of describing it |

`EML151` catches three shapes: `Unique identifier for X`, the column name in
prose (`Status for Client`), and a template sentence (`X is a business record in
…`). It is deliberately narrow, so real help that happens to be short — *The day
this offer expires.* — does not fire. It exists because coverage can be complete
and the help still worthless: a published model once carried help on all 91 of
its entities and all 551 of its columns, and 699 of those lines were of exactly
these shapes.

**The primary key needs no help, and `EML153` does not ask for any.** It is a
generated uuid, read-only on every form, and the only sentence anybody could
write about it restates its name — which is what `EML151` then reports. Leave it
out.

**What to say, per kind of column:**

| Column | Say |
|---|---|
| A reference (`_id`) | what the reference is *for* — "the ward this bed stands in", never "the ward id" |
| An enum-bound column | what each value means to the business, because the dictionary lists the values and nothing says what choosing one *does* |
| A lifecycle column | which moves are possible from which state — the state machine enforces a topology no form can show |
| A money column | gross or net, which currency, and what it is compared against |
| A date | which business event it records, and what is true before it is set |
| A flag | what turning it on permits or prevents, and who may do so |

A delivery missing help is incomplete even though the checker returns zero
errors — §10's checklist asks for all three codes.
- **`%%index <E>(<a>[, <b>]) [unique]`** becomes a real index. Add one for every
  column combination the business searches or filters on, and no more — every
  index is paid for on every write.
- **`%%category`** groups entities on the generated dashboard. `name` is the only
  required key; `entities` is a comma-separated list. Only `;` separates keys.
  **There is no shorthand**: `%%category Sources: DataSource, SchemaEntity` reads
  perfectly well and declares nothing, because the parser requires `name:` and
  skips the line without it — the grouping is lost and every entity in it falls
  into the default `General` category. Reported as `EML154`.

**An `icon:` names a lucide icon, and a wrong name is silent.** `%%category
icon:` reaches `sys_category.icon` and is drawn beside the category's heading on
the dashboard; `%%entity icon:` reaches `sys_table.icon` and is drawn on the
entity's own card. Three spellings all resolve — `LayoutGrid`, `layout_grid` and
`layout-grid` are the same icon — so write whichever reads best. What does *not*
resolve is a name lucide does not have: it is **not** a diagnostic, because the
checker does not carry lucide's catalogue, and the application draws a
placeholder in its place. `icon: flask` is the trap — lucide has no `flask`, it
has `flask-conical` — and it sat uncaught in this project's own hospital example
for months, drawing a placeholder where the Diagnostics heading's icon should
have been. Check a name at https://lucide.dev/icons before writing it.

### 3.7 The Application Dictionary — what your ERD becomes on every screen

The generated application does not hard-code its forms. Every table, column,
window, tab, field, section and lookup is a row in an **Application
Dictionary**, and the running interface reads those rows at runtime — which is
why a field can be added to a live application without a deployment. **You never
write dictionary rows, and there is no `%%dictionary` directive.** The dictionary
is derived, one way, from what you declare — so "filling in the dictionary"
means declaring the model precisely enough for every derived value to be the
right one. Nothing after authoring adds a value you left out.

#### 3.7.1 Three layers, and where each value comes from

| Layer | Rows | What it answers | Where its values come from in your model |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Storage** | `sys_table`, `sys_column`, `sys_reference`, `sys_ref_list` | What is stored, and as what kind of value | Entity blocks, attribute types and modifiers, `%%enum` + `%%field … enum:`, `%%entity … help:`, `%%field … help:` |
| **Screen** | `sys_window`, `sys_tab`, `sys_field`, `sys_field_group` | Where a value is shown, beside what, under which heading | One window and tab per entity (a line item's tab sits in its parent's window); **`%%section`** for the headings, rows and columns |
| **Navigation and access** | `sys_category`, `sys_access`, the role tables | Where an entity is found, and who may see it | `%%category`, `%%rbac` |

| You write | It becomes |
|---|---|
| an entity block | `sys_table` (the `bus_<snake>` table), one `sys_window` (unless it is a line item) and one `sys_tab` |
| an attribute | `sys_column` and a `sys_field` on the entity's tab |
| its type, alias and modifiers | `sys_column.sys_reference_id` — **the control a person gets** (§3.7.2) |
| `%%enum` + `%%field <E>.<c> enum:` | a `List` reference with one `sys_ref_list` row per value |
| `%%entity <E> help:` | `sys_table.description` — and the opening of that entity's section of the generated manual |
| `%%field <E>.<c> help:` | `sys_column.description` — the hint under the control, and the column's row in the manual |
| `%%section entity: <E>; name: …; help: …; rows: …` | one `sys_field_group` per section (heading, help, two columns) and each field's group, order, row, column and span (§3.7.6) |
| `%%entity <Child> parent: <Parent>` | the child's tab inside the parent's window at level 1, linked on the child's foreign key (§3.5.1) |
| `%%category name: …; entities: …` | `sys_category`, the dashboard's grouping |
| `%%entity <E> icon:` | `sys_table.icon` — the card, window heading and navigation icon |
| `%%rbac … .read` | which roles' `sys_access` rows reach the entity, and so whose dashboard shows it |

#### 3.7.2 Reference types — the control each column gets

The property that decides what a user actually sees is the column's **reference
type**, `sys_column.sys_reference_id`. It is derived in this order, and the first
rule that matches wins:

1. The entity's primary key gets **ID** (13) — the key, hidden on every form.
2. A column **marked `FK` and named `_id` / `_by` that resolves to a declared
   entity** gets **Table Direct** (19) — a lookup on the parent table (§3.7.3).
3. A column bound by `%%field <E>.<c> enum: <Enum>` gets that enum's **List**
   reference (id 1000 or above) — a dropdown of exactly those values.
