```js
import { pathToFileURL } from "node:url";

const dir = mkdtempSync(join(tmpdir(), "eml-"));
for (const name of ["checker.js", "fixer.js"]) {
  const response = await fetch(`https://www.appwithai.org/guide/${name}`);
  writeFileSync(join(dir, name), await response.text());
}
const { check, formatReport } = await import(pathToFileURL(join(dir, "checker.js")).href);
const { checkAndFix } = await import(pathToFileURL(join(dir, "fixer.js")).href);

const report = checkAndFix(readFileSync("my-business.mmd", "utf8"));
console.log(formatReport(check(report.source)));
```

Both files must land in the same directory: `fixer.js` imports `checker.js` from
beside itself.

### 8.5 Is the model *finished*? — the checklist audit

A clean report and a finished model are different things, and the gap between
them is where delivered models actually fail.

Nothing in the checker requires a model to *have* anything. A single entity with
a primary key and a name is a valid EML document: no state machine, no saga, no
hook, no `%%action`, no `%%rbac` line, not one word of help text — zero errors,
zero warnings, and the generator will build it. What comes out is a grid of text
boxes that every user can see all of, with no lifecycle, no rules and no
security, and the report said it was fine. The three warnings that do fire
(`EML146`, `EML152`, `EML153`) are advisory: `formatReport` ends such a run with
*"the generator accepts this model"*, which is true and is not the same as
*"this model is done"*.

So there is a second published runner, beside the first and resolved the same
way:

```sh
curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/audit-model.mjs
node audit-model.mjs my-business.mmd
```

It scores the mechanical half of §1.2's file contract and §10's checklist —
twenty-three checks — and its last line is the score:

```
23 passed, 0 failed
```

Exit `0` when every check passed, `1` when one or more failed, `2` when it could
not run. `--quiet` prints the score line alone; `--base <dir-or-url>` is the same
flag `check-model.mjs` has, and the offline rows of §8.4 apply unchanged.

What it holds a model to, and what a clean checker run would not have told you:

| It checks | Because a clean report does not mean |
|---|---|
| The file's name, its first line, no Markdown anywhere in it | The bytes are a `.mmd` a Mermaid viewer renders (§1.2) |
| Every entity has a primary key; every `FK` ends `_id`; **every `_id`/`_by` column carries the `FK` modifier** | The reference is a `Table Direct` lookup rather than a silently downgraded text box (§3.7) |
| Every `status`/`state`/`stage` column is bound by `%%field … enum:` | The control is a List rather than free text the state machine cannot act on (§3.7) |
| At least one `kind: state` workflow, each with an initial transition and a terminal state | The records have a lifecycle at all (§5.2) |
| `%%action`, `kind: saga`, `%%hook` and `%%rbac` are all present | The model decides, runs and restricts something — rather than being an ERD with diagrams beside it |
| Every entity laid out in `%%section` rows, every column but the key placed, every section with help | The form is headed sections of two-column rows someone designed, not one flat list (`EML170`, `EML172`, `EML177`) |
| Help on every entity and every column, **none of it restating its own name** | The application and its generated manual say something. `Status for Client.` is complete coverage and worthless (`EML151`, `EML152`, `EML153`) |
| Every declared line item is out of every `%%category`, and every candidate is reported | The dashboard does not carry a card listing every invoice line ever written (§3.5.1, `EML149`, `EML150`) |
| `checkAndFix` then two `check` passes over the repaired bytes, all clean | The bytes you are delivering are the bytes that passed (§1.3) |

Three of those — the `FK` modifier, the enum binding, and help that says
something — are the ones worth re-reading, because each is a warning the
generator proceeds past after quietly getting the application wrong.

**It is a scorer, not a second checker.** Every diagnostic it reads comes from
`checker.js`; it adds no codes of its own. And it cannot tell you the model says
what the business meant — only that nothing in it is mechanically unfinished.
`EML149` candidates are *printed* rather than counted against the score, because
whether something is a line item is a question about the business and a candidate
you have considered and rejected is a legitimate answer.

**Run it before you deliver, and report its score beside the checker's counts.**
A delivery that says *"0 errors, 0 warnings"* and nothing else is not wrong, and
it is not the whole truth about the file either.

---

## 9. A complete worked example

Every construct in this specification, in one checker-clean document. These
bytes, saved as `acme-dance-studio.mmd`, are a finished deliverable: no headings,
no prose, no explanation outside the language itself. This is the shape of what
you hand over — imitate it exactly, at whatever size the business needs.

```mermaid
%%meta name: Acme Dance Studio
%%meta kind: erd
%%meta version: 1.0.0

%%category name: Scheduling; description: Classes, the rooms that host them and who teaches; icon: CalendarClock; entities: DanceClass, Room, Instructor
%%category name: Membership; description: Members and their bookings; icon: Users; default: true; entities: Member, Booking

%% Every entity belongs to a functional role. `read` is what decides it, so
%% signing in as reception gives you the desk's application rather than the
%% studio's. `manager` reads everything because managing is that job.
%%rbac role:reception|manager|instructor on DanceClass.read
%%rbac role:reception|manager on Room.read
%%rbac role:manager|instructor on Instructor.read
%%rbac role:reception|manager on Member.read
%%rbac role:reception|manager|instructor on Booking.read

%%enum ClassStatus: scheduled, running, completed, cancelled
%%enum BookingStatus: requested, confirmed, attended, cancelled, no_show
%%enum MemberTier: trial, standard, unlimited

erDiagram
    Instructor {
        string  id PK
        string  full_name
        email   email UK
        phone   phone OPTIONAL
        boolean is_active
    }
    Room {
        string  id PK
        string  name UK
        integer capacity
    }
    Member {
        string  id PK
        string  full_name
        email   email UK
        string  tier
        date    joined_on
        integer credits
    }
    DanceClass {
        string   id PK
        string   instructor_id FK
        string   room_id FK
        string   title
        string   status
        datetime starts_at
        integer  capacity
        integer  booked_count
        money    price OPTIONAL
    }
    Booking {
        string   id PK
        string   member_id FK
        string   dance_class_id FK
        string   status
        datetime requested_at
        text     cancellation_reason OPTIONAL
    }

    Instructor ||--o{ DanceClass : "teaches"
    Room       ||--o{ DanceClass : "hosts"
    Member     ||--o{ Booking : "makes"
    DanceClass ||--o{ Booking : "receives"

%%field DanceClass.status enum: ClassStatus
%%field Booking.status enum: BookingStatus
%%field Member.tier enum: MemberTier

%%index DanceClass(instructor_id, starts_at)
%%index Booking(dance_class_id, status)

%%entity Instructor help: Somebody who teaches at the studio. Instructors are booked against classes, so one who leaves is deactivated rather than deleted: their past classes stay attributed and the attendance history stays readable.
%%field Instructor.full_name help: The name on the timetable, which is how members choose a class. Use the name the studio advertises rather than the one on the contract.
%%field Instructor.email help: Where the schedule and any cancellation reach them, and how they sign in. Unique, because it identifies the person.
%%field Instructor.phone help: A number reception can call on the morning of a class. Optional, and the reason a class is covered rather than cancelled when somebody is ill.
%%field Instructor.is_active help: Whether they are currently teaching. Cleared instead of deleting; an inactive instructor should not appear when a new class is scheduled.

%%entity Room help: A physical studio a class is held in. Rooms are the constraint the timetable is built against — two classes cannot share one at the same hour — and their capacity is the ceiling on every class booked into them.
%%field Room.name help: What the room is called on the timetable and on the door. Unique, because a member navigating the building relies on it being unambiguous.
%%field Room.capacity help: The most people the room legally holds, instructor included. It is a fire regulation rather than a preference, and no class may be booked above it.

%%entity Member help: Somebody who books classes. The membership record carries the tier that decides what they may book and the credit balance a trial member spends, so it exists before any booking does.
%%field Member.full_name help: The name reception greets them by and the name on the class register.
%%field Member.email help: Where confirmations and cancellations are sent, and how the member signs in. Unique across members, so one person is one history.
%%field Member.tier help: trial — pay-as-you-go from a credit balance; standard — a set number of classes a month; unlimited — no cap. The tier is what the admission rule reads before allowing a booking.
%%field Member.joined_on help: When the membership began. It is what a length-of-relationship report is built on and what a renewal date is computed from.
%%field Member.credits help: Classes a trial member has left to spend. The admission rule refuses a trial member with none, which is the only thing standing between a free trial and an unlimited one.

%%entity DanceClass help: One session at one time in one room with one instructor. The class is what a member books onto and what the studio is paid for; its booked count is maintained by the booking saga rather than typed, because two people booking at once must not both be told there was a seat.
%%field DanceClass.instructor_id help: Who is teaching. Changing it is a substitution, and members who booked for a named instructor generally expect to be told.
%%field DanceClass.room_id help: Where it is held. It caps the class's own capacity and is what a member is looking for when they arrive.
%%field DanceClass.title help: The class as it appears on the timetable — the style and the level a member is choosing between. "Beginners' salsa", not "Class 14".
%%field DanceClass.status help: scheduled — open for bookings; running — under way; completed — taught, and countable in attendance; cancelled — called off, and every booking on it has to be moved or refunded. Only the moves the lifecycle draws are allowed.
%%field DanceClass.starts_at help: When the session begins, in the studio's own time zone. It orders the timetable and it is what a reminder is sent against.
%%field DanceClass.capacity help: The most bookings this session will take, at or below the room's limit. Set lower than the room where the style needs floor space.
%%field DanceClass.booked_count help: How many places are taken. Maintained by the booking saga, and the figure the admission rule compares against capacity — a count that drifts is how a class comes to be oversold.
%%field DanceClass.price help: What a member pays for this session if they are not drawing on a tier or a credit. Empty where the class is included in the membership.

%%entity Booking help: One member's place on one session, from the moment they ask for it to the moment they turn up or do not. It is what capacity is counted against, so a cancellation frees a place and a no-show does not — which is the distinction the whole waiting list depends on.
%%field Booking.member_id help: Who is booked. It is what the class register is built from and who a cancellation notice is sent to.
%%field Booking.dance_class_id help: The session being booked. Its capacity and booked count are what the admission rule checks before the booking is accepted.
%%field Booking.status help: requested — asked for, not yet accepted; confirmed — the place is held; attended — the member came; cancelled — the place is released; no_show — the place was held and wasted, which is what a repeat-offender policy is built on.
%%field Booking.requested_at help: When the member asked, not when reception confirmed. It orders the waiting list, so it is the only fair basis for who gets a freed place.
%%field Booking.cancellation_reason help: Why the place was given up, in the member's words. It is the difference between a member the studio should call and one who simply changed their mind.
%%section entity: Instructor; name: Instructor; help: Who teaches, how the studio reaches them, and whether they can be timetabled.; rows: full_name, is_active | email, phone
%%section entity: Room; name: Room; help: The studio room and how many dancers it safely holds.; rows: name, capacity
%%section entity: Member; name: Member; help: Who dances here, how to reach them, and the membership they hold.; rows: full_name, email | tier, joined_on | credits
%%section entity: DanceClass; name: Class; help: What is taught, by whom, where, and whether it is going ahead.; rows: title, status | instructor_id, room_id
%%section entity: DanceClass; name: Session; help: When it runs, how many it takes and have booked, and what a drop-in pays.; rows: starts_at, price | capacity, booked_count
%%section entity: Booking; name: Booking; help: Who booked which class, where the booking stands, and why it was cancelled if it was.; rows: member_id, dance_class_id | status, requested_at | cancellation_reason

%%meta name: Booking Admission
%%meta kind: rules
%%rule bookingAdmission on Booking event: beforeCreate priority: 10
flowchart TD
    A([Start: Booking requested]) --> B{class is full?}
    B -->|Yes| C[Refuse: no seats left]
    B -->|No| D{member tier == trial?}
    D -->|Yes| E{member credits > 0?}
    E -->|No| F[Refuse: trial credits exhausted]
    E -->|Yes| G[Admit and spend one credit]
    D -->|No| H[Admit]
    C --> Z([End: Admission decided])
    F --> Z
    G --> Z
    H --> Z

    %%action refuseFullClass validation-error when: status == "requested" and booked_count >= capacity message: This class is full — offer the member the waitlist
    %%action confirmBooking trigger-workflow when: status == "confirmed" workflow: ClassFillTracking message: Booking confirmed — updating the class headcount

%%meta name: Booking Lifecycle
%%meta kind: workflow
%%workflow BookingLifecycle entity: Booking kind: state
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> requested
    requested --> confirmed : confirm
    requested --> cancelled : reject
    confirmed --> attended  : check_in
    confirmed --> cancelled : cancel
    confirmed --> no_show   : mark_absent
    attended  --> [*]
    cancelled --> [*]
    no_show   --> [*]

    %%rbac role:reception|manager on Booking.confirm
    %%rbac role:manager on Booking.cancel
    %%rbac role:manager on Booking.delete

%%meta name: Class Fill Tracking
%%meta kind: workflow
%%workflow ClassFillTracking entity: Booking kind: saga trigger: rule
flowchart TD
    A([Booking confirmed]) --> B(Count the seat)
    B --> C[Raise the class headcount]
    C --> Z([Headcount updated])

    %%step B Formula target: seatCount source: booked_count operation: add operand: 1
    %%step C UpdateEntity entity: DanceClass targetField: dance_class_id field: booked_count source: seatCount
```

---

## 10. Before you deliver — the checklist

**Most of this list is machine-checkable, so do not walk it by hand.** Items 1-4
and 6-17 are what `audit-model.mjs` scores — twenty-three checks, one command, the
same engines the checker runs (§8.5):

```sh
curl -sO https://www.appwithai.org/guide/audit-model.mjs
node audit-model.mjs my-business.mmd
```

`23 passed, 0 failed` and exit `0` is the state to deliver in. Read the list
anyway for the three items no script can answer — 5, 7 and 18 are about whether
the model matches the business — and for the reasoning behind the ones it can.

**The file itself**

1. There *is* a file, and it is Mermaid — not a document describing one (§1.0).
2. Its first non-blank line begins with `%%`, and `%%meta name:` is declared
   before the first `erDiagram` / `flowchart` / `stateDiagram-v2`.
3. It contains no Markdown, no fences, no prose outside `%%` comment lines.
4. It is one file, named `<business-name>.mmd`, and it renders in a Mermaid
   viewer.

**The model**

5. Every entity from the agreed roster (§1.1.5) is in the document — and, for a
   change, every entity, column, section, help line, `%%rbac` line and `%%report`
   of the model you were given, unless the user asked for it to go (§1.3.3).
6. Every entity has a primary key you chose, declares each column once
   (`EML112`), and declares none of the seven the generator adds — `id` aside,
   `version`, the audit pair and the soft-delete pair are already there
   (§3.1, `EML103`).
7. Every entity that something references has a `name`, `title` or `code`
   column — that is what a lookup and a grid show in place of the uuid (§3.7).
8. Every foreign key ends `_id`, **carries the `FK` modifier**, and has a
   matching relationship line — the modifier is what makes it a `Table Direct`
   lookup in the Application Dictionary rather than a text box (§3.7).
9. Every status column, and every other column with a closed vocabulary, has a
   `%%enum` **and** a `%%field … enum:` binding it — without the binding the
   dictionary records free text (§3.7).
10. **Every entity carries `%%entity <E> help:` and every column carries
   `%%field <E>.<col> help:`** — no exceptions, including the self-evident ones,
   and the primary key the one thing that needs none. That text is the whole of
   the application's help *and* the whole of its generated manual, and no later
   pass adds it (§3.6, §3.7). **It has to be domain knowledge, not the name in a
   sentence**: `Status for Client.` passes a coverage check and tells a reader
   nothing. Clear every `EML151` (help that restates its subject), `EML152` (an
   entity with none) and `EML153` (columns with none).
11. **Every entity's form is laid out** in `%%section` rows — headed sections
   of one or two columns per row, every column but the primary key placed
   exactly once, each section with `help:` saying what that part of the form is
   for, named for what the person is doing rather than the kind of column it
   holds (§3.7.6). Clear every `EML170`, `EML172` and `EML177`.
12. **Every line item is declared as one.** Go through the entities and ask of
   each: is this a thing in its own right, or part of another thing? Every
   invoice line, order line, prescription item and delivery line gets
   `%%entity <Child> parent: <Parent>`, and is left out of `%%category`
   (§3.5.1). Missing it puts a card on the dashboard listing every line ever
   written, which is a screen nobody opens — and leaves the parent record with
   no sign of its own lines. The checker names every candidate it can see as
   `EML149`; walk each one and either declare the parent or decide against it,
   and clear any `EML150` by taking the child out of its category.
13. Every entity with a status has a `kind: state` workflow, with an initial
   transition and a terminal state.
14. Every rule that must *do* something has an `%%action` — not just a flowchart.
15. Every cross-entity effect is a hook, an action, or a saga step.
16. Every restricted operation and transition has a `%%rbac` directive.
17. Every entity is named by at least one `%%rbac … .read` directive, so it
   belongs to a functional role — and every role that may act on an entity can
   also read it (§6). A model where one role sees all forty tables is the same
   application once, not four times.

18. **If the model carries `%%report` directives, more than one role has them.**
   A reporting layer that answers one person's questions is that person's saved
   query. Walk the roles on the `%%rbac` matrix: a role with a read-list and no
   report can see its records and cannot ask anything about them. Reports are
   optional — a model without any is complete — but a model with exactly one
   role's worth is half-finished rather than economical.

**The handover**

19. Exactly one file is being handed over, and it ends `.mmd` — no companion
    specification document, report or README (§1.0).
20. `check(source)` returns `ok: true`, run three times over the file's exact
    bytes, the last two over unchanged bytes — `node check-model.mjs <file>.mmd`
    is those three passes and exits `0` — and you reached that state by looping
    check → fix → check until the report was empty, for at least 10 cycles or
    until it came back clean, whichever was first (§1.3) — or you have said
    plainly that the checker could not be run and walked this list by hand
    instead (§1.3).
21. Warnings are cleared, or each remaining one is explained to the user.
22. **`node audit-model.mjs <file>.mmd` exits `0`** — every mechanical item
    above, scored rather than remembered (§8.5). A clean checker run does not
    imply this one: a model with no `%%rbac`, no state machine and no help text
    is 0 errors and 0 warnings, and it is not finished. If a check fails and you
    are leaving it that way, say which and why.
23. The file the user receives is the file you validated, delivered as a
    download, with the premises and roster (or, for a change, the before-and-after
    inventory), the checker counts **and the
    audit score** beside it in the reply — not inside the file (§1.4).
